pos: adj. (of great price, highly esteemed; rendering Hebrew yaqar, Greek timios)
etymology: From Latin pretiosus, from pretium, price. Scripture prices strange things precious: blood, promises, trials, and the deaths of saints.
biblical_def: Precious means valued at great price. Peter owns the word: redemption came “with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish” (1Pe 1:19); believers are given “exceeding great and precious promises” (2Pe 1:4); and the whole difference between belief and unbelief is an appraisal — “unto you therefore which believe he is precious” (1Pe 2:7). The psalmist adds the appraisal from God's side: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psa 116:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines precious as of great price, costly, of great value, highly esteemed — citing the precious blood and the precious faith of the apostolic epistles.
webster_full: PRECIOUS, a. Of great price; costly; as a precious stone.
2. Of great value or worth; very valuable.
3. Highly esteemed; much valued; dear.
scriptures: But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot:
Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.
Unto you therefore which believe he is precious: but unto them which be disobedient, the stone which the builders disallowed, the same is made the head of the corner,
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: A word worn smooth on trinkets and toddlers while its biblical appraisals invert the market: the age prices platform and portfolio precious, and blood, promises, and dying saints cheap.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's valuation is explicitly comparative: not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, but with precious blood. The metals every economy trusts are filed under corruptible; one death outside Jerusalem is priced beyond them all. A church discipled by the market's appraisals will handle the blood casually and the budget reverently — and its liturgy will show which it finds precious.

Psalm 116:15 corrects the other ledger. The world writes off a saint's death as loss, statistics, an ending; God prices it precious — the arrival of one for whom Christ paid. And 1 Peter 2:7 makes the appraisal the dividing line of mankind: to believers, He is precious; to the disobedient, a stone to stumble over. Every soul prices Christ, and is priced by its pricing.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaqar (H3368), precious, rare, weighty; Greek timios (G5093), held at high price — the blood of Christ, and the fruit the husbandman waits for.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaqar (H3368) — precious, costly, rare; the precious sons of Zion (Lam 4:2) and how precious are thy thoughts unto me, O God (Psa 139:17).
Greek timios (G5093) — valued, honored, costly; precious blood (1Pe 1:19), precious promises (2Pe 1:4), precious faith (2Pe 1:1).
usage: “Redeemed… with the precious blood of Christ” — the price silver and gold could not touch.
“Exceeding great and precious promises” — the believer's portfolio.
“Unto you therefore which believe he is precious” — every soul is known by its appraisal of Christ.

etymology: Never-the-less: not the less for all that. The Bible's great hinge-word, on which prayers, obediences, and Gethsemane itself turn.
biblical_def: Nevertheless concedes everything and surrenders nothing. Peter's empty nets: “Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net” (Luk 5:5). Asaph's envy-sick heart: “Nevertheless I am continually with thee” (Psa 73:23). The apostasy of professors: “Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure” (2Ti 2:19). And the darkest garden in history: “nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” (Luk 22:42). Faith's grammar lives in this adverb — the facts admitted, the obedience anyway.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nevertheless as not the less; notwithstanding; that is, in opposition to any thing, or without regarding it.
webster_full: NEVERTHELESS, adv. Not the less; notwithstanding; that is, in opposition to any thing, or without regarding it.
scriptures: Luk 5:5
And Simon answering said unto him, Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.
Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand.
Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.
Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.
corruption_summary: Positivity culture forbids the first half of the word (admit nothing negative) and autonomy culture forbids the second (submit to nothing anyway) — between them, the hinge of faith rusts unused.
corruption_paragraphs: Every nevertheless has two chambers: an honest concession and an overriding commitment. Modern religious optimism amputates the concession — toil-all-night-and-take-nothing must be reframed, never admitted — producing a faith that cannot survive an honest bad night. Peter's obedience is stronger precisely because his report is bleak: all night, nothing. Faith is not the refusal to count empty nets; it is letting down the net after counting them, at His word.

Gethsemane spends the word's full price. The cup is really dreaded; the if-it-be-possible is really prayed; and then the hinge turns: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done. Every lesser surrender borrows from that one. A generation catechized to treat its own will as sacred has lost the word's second chamber — and with it, the only prayer that ever carried a soul through a garden at night.
roots_summary: Greek plen (G4133), howbeit, but, nevertheless — the adversative that turns Gethsemane; elsewhere simple de carries the same holy pivot.
roots_lines: Greek plen (G4133) — but, nevertheless, notwithstanding; Luke 22:42, and rejoice not that the spirits are subject unto you, but rather rejoice… (Luk 10:20).
usage: “Nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net” — the facts counted, the obedience anyway.
“Nevertheless I am continually with thee” — the psalm turns from envy to presence on one adverb.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” — the hinge on which redemption swung.

pos: adj., adv. (surpassing, beyond measure; rendering Hebrew meod, Greek huperballo)
etymology: From Latin excedere, to go beyond. The KJV's favorite intensifier for realities that overflow their containers — reward, power, glory, joy.
biblical_def: Exceeding marks what surpasses measure. God covenants Himself to Abram as “thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward” (Gen 15:1). Paul stacks the word on grace's power — able to do “exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think” (Eph 3:20) — and on glory's weight: affliction light and momentary, working “a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2Co 4:17). Jude closes with presentation “faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy” (Jude 24). The word exists because God habitually overruns the containers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exceeding as great in extent, quantity or duration; surpassing — and as an adverb of intensity, in a very great degree.
webster_full: EXCEEDING, ppr. Going beyond; surpassing; excelling; outdoing.
2. a. Great in extent, quantity or duration; very extensive.
3. adv. In a very great degree; unusually; as, exceeding rich.
scriptures: Gen 15:1
After these things the word of the LORD came unto Abram in a vision, saying, Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.
Eph 3:20
Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,
For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;
Jude 24
Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,
corruption_summary: An age of inflation without magnitude — everything awesome, epic, unbelievable — has spent the superlatives and lost the Referent they were coined for.
corruption_paragraphs: The KJV deploys exceeding with an economy modern hype cannot afford: it is reserved for what genuinely bursts measurement — the reward that is God Himself, the power that answers beyond asking and thinking, the glory that outweighs affliction by an order the sentence strains to say (a far more exceeding and eternal weight). When every burrito is epic, the language has no register left for Ephesians 3:20; recovering the word means re-learning proportion, which is a spiritual discipline before it is a stylistic one.

Notice too where Scripture does not put the word: possessions are never the exceeding great reward; the LORD is. Abram had just refused the spoils of Sodom when the word came — the shield and the reward arrive precisely where the portfolio was declined. The prosperity inversion prices the gifts exceeding and the Giver modest; Genesis 15:1 prices the Giver as the reward, and everything else as footnote.
roots_summary: Hebrew meod (H3966), muchness, exceedingly — the very-very of Hebrew emphasis; Greek huperballo (G5235), to throw beyond — Paul's surpassing word for grace, power, and glory.
roots_lines: Hebrew meod (H3966) — exceedingly, greatly; behold, it was very good (Gen 1:31) carries it, and Abram's exceeding great reward doubles it.
Greek huperballo (G5235) — to surpass, exceed; the exceeding riches of his grace (Eph 2:7), the exceeding greatness of his power (Eph 1:19).
usage: “I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward” — the Giver Himself is the payout.
“Exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think” — grace overruns both prayer and imagination.
“A far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” — the scales that make affliction light.

etymology: From Latin falsus, deceived, counterfeit. Scripture's false is never merely mistaken; it is manufactured against the truth.
biblical_def: False names the counterfeit. The ninth commandment forbids the false witness (Exo 20:16); our Lord warns of “false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing” (Mat 7:15) and of “false Christs, and false prophets” showing great signs (Mat 24:24); Paul unmasks “false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ” (2Co 11:13). The adjective's biblical habit is chilling: it attaches most readily to religious nouns — witness, prophet, christ, apostle, brethren, teachers. The counterfeit industry works where the currency is most precious.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines false as not true, not conformable to fact; counterfeit, forged, not genuine — hypocritical, deceitful, treacherous.
webster_full: FALSE, a. Not true; not conformable to fact; expressing what is contrary to that which exists.
2. Counterfeit; forged; not genuine; as false coin.
3. Not faithful; treacherous; perfidious; deceitful.
scriptures: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive the very elect.
For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ.
corruption_summary: A culture that has retired the category — your truth and my truth, no false anything — is the softest market a false prophet ever worked.
corruption_paragraphs: Sheep's clothing is a supply-chain detail worth pondering: the counterfeit dresses in the target's fabric. False prophets do not arrive advertising wolfhood; they arrive fluent in the flock's vocabulary, warm in its manner, quoting its Book. Christ's test is therefore not the wool but the fruit — by their fruits ye shall know them — which requires the one discipline relativism forbids: judging teaching by a fixed standard over time.

The ninth commandment locates the false at the root: the tongue bearing false witness against a neighbour. Before there are false prophets there are false words about persons — and an age that has industrialized the false witness (the misquote, the edit, the pile-on) while abolishing false as a doctrinal category has exactly inverted Sinai. God, who cannot lie, hates the false in testimony and in theology for the same reason: both counterfeit His image-bearing speech.
roots_summary: Hebrew sheqer (H8267), lie, falsehood — the false witness's word; Greek pseudes (G5571) and its compounds — pseudo-prophets, pseudo-christs, pseudo-apostles — the New Testament's counterfeit prefix.
roots_lines: Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — lie, deception, falsehood; thou shalt not bear false witness (Exo 20:16), and the prophets prophesy falsely (Jer 5:31).
Greek pseudoprophetes (G5578) — false prophet; Matthew 7:15, 24:24, and the beast's companion in Revelation.
Greek pseudapostolos (G5570) — false apostle; 2 Corinthians 11:13, deceitful workers in borrowed light.
usage: “Thou shalt not bear false witness” — the counterfeit forbidden at the root, in testimony.
“Beware of false prophets… in sheep's clothing” — the counterfeit dresses in the target's fabric.
“False apostles… transforming themselves” — the disguise reaches even the highest office.

etymology: Old English latost, superlative of late. The Greek behind it, eschatos, names the whole doctrine of last things — eschatology.
biblical_def: Last is Scripture's word for finality, and it belongs supremely to Christ: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last” (Rev 22:13). It stamps the calendar — “in the last days perilous times shall come” (2Ti 3:1) — and the resurrection's trumpet: “at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised” (1Co 15:52). And it overturns every human ranking: “So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen” (Mat 20:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines last as that comes after all the others; the latest; hindmost — and in Scripture, the lowest place, which the kingdom keeps promoting.
webster_full: LAST, a. That comes after all the others; the latest; applied to time.
2. That follows all the others; that is behind all the others in place; hindmost.
3. Utmost; as the last degree.
scriptures: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.
This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come.
corruption_summary: Eschatology traded for optimization — a civilization planning quarters, not ends — while the church that should live from the last day frets over the news cycle like everyone else.
corruption_paragraphs: The first-and-last title does the heavy lifting most readers miss: history is bracketed by a Person. Not by heat death, not by progress, not by markets — by the same Christ at both ends. That bracketing is why the believer can read 2 Timothy 3's perilous last days without panic; perilous times are inside the brackets, and the Last One has already spoken from beyond them. A church addicted to crisis has forgotten which bracket it lives toward.

Meanwhile the kingdom's ranking algorithm remains scandalous: the last shall be first. Every institution, including religious ones, sorts by visibility, seniority, platform; the vineyard's paymaster works from the other end of the line. The parable does not abolish reward; it abolishes calculation — and the workers most confident of their standing hear the coldest sentence. Living toward the last day means letting the last trump, not the leaderboard, set the sort order.
roots_summary: Hebrew acharon (H314), after, latter, last — the latter day in which the Redeemer stands upon the earth; Greek eschatos (G2078), last — the root of eschatology, and a title of Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew acharon (H314) — latter, last; I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth (Job 19:25).
Greek eschatos (G2078) — last, final; the last trump (1Co 15:52), the last days (2Ti 3:1), the first and the last (Rev 22:13).
usage: “I am… the first and the last” — history bracketed by a Person.
“At the last trump… the dead shall be raised” — finality with a resurrection inside it.
“So the last shall be first, and the first last” — the kingdom's sort order.

pos: adv. (not ever, at no time; rendering Greek ou me, the emphatic double negative)
etymology: Old English næfre, not-ever. In the Greek of the promises it is often ou me — a doubled negative the KJV renders never, in no wise, by no means.
biblical_def: Never is the adverb of divine commitment. “My sheep… shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand” (Joh 10:28). “He that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst” (Joh 6:35). “I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” (Heb 13:5) — in the Greek, negatives stacked five deep. And the psalmist's assurance: God “shall never suffer the righteous to be moved” (Psa 55:22). Where God says never, eternity is being promised in grammar.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines never as not ever, not at any time — the total negative of time; Scripture's nevers are total negatives sworn by the Eternal.
webster_full: NEVER, adv. Not ever; not at any time; at no time.
2. In no degree; not at all.
scriptures: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand.
Joh 6:35
And Jesus said unto them, I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic gospel that dare not say never — every promise hedged to probably, every assurance to for-now — leaves saints insecure precisely where Christ spoke double negatives.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greek of John 10:28 is ou me apolontai eis ton aiona — they shall not, not perish, unto the age. Christ reached for the strongest negation His language owned and then added eternity to it. Systems in which the sheep can, after all, perish must read the sentence as enthusiasm rather than covenant; but the verse's own architecture — given by the Father, held in two hands, never perishing — is built as security. Assurance is not presumption when it stands on a never Christ spoke.

Hebrews 13:5 aims the never at money's throne: be content with such things as ye have, FOR he hath said, I will never leave thee. Contentment's logic runs through presence — the wallet may thin, the Presence will not. A believer hedging that promise back to probably has traded the strongest sentence in his possession for the anxiety the verse was written to end.
roots_summary: Greek ou me (G3364), the emphatic double negative — never, in no wise, by no means; the grammar of covenant security throughout the promises of Christ.
roots_lines: Greek ou me (G3364) — the doubled negative of absolute denial; shall never perish (Joh 10:28), shall never hunger (Joh 6:35), I will in no wise cast out (Joh 6:37).
Hebrews 13:5 stacks ou me with additional negatives — I will never, never leave thee; never, never, never forsake thee — five negations in one promise.
usage: “They shall never perish” — the strongest negation Greek owns, plus eternity.
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee” — five negatives deep in the original.
“He shall never suffer the righteous to be moved” — the psalmist's cast-thy-burden warrant.

pos: adv., adj. (at dawn, betimes; rendering Hebrew shachar)
etymology: Old English ærlice, before the usual time. In Scripture the hour of seeking, of divine help, and of the empty tomb.
biblical_def: Early is the seeking hour. David in the wilderness: “O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee” (Psa 63:1). Wisdom's standing promise: “I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me” (Pro 8:17). The besieged city's timetable: “God shall help her, and that right early” (Psa 46:5). And the church's greatest morning: “very early in the morning the first day of the week, they came unto the sepulchre at the rising of the sun” (Mar 16:2) — and found it empty.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines early as in advance of something else in time, soon, betimes — the first part of the day; Scripture makes it the first part of the heart.
webster_full: EARLY, adv. Soon; in good season; betimes; as, to rise early.
EARLY, a. In advance of something else in time; prior in time; forward.
scriptures: Psa 63:1

A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is;
Pro 8:17
I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me.
Psa 46:5
God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early.
Mar 16:2
And very early in the morning the first day of the week, they came unto the sepulchre at the rising of the sun.
corruption_summary: The first hour surrendered to the feed — a generation that seeks its phone early and wonders why God feels distant by noon.
corruption_paragraphs: The biblical writers treat the day's first hour as disputed territory that must be claimed. The Hebrew of Psalm 63:1 is a verb formed from dawn itself — I will dawn-seek thee — and the prophets add the LORD's own habit, rising up early and sending His messengers, daily rising up early and sending. What fills the first hour discipleship the rest; the modern morning liturgy of scroll-before-rising is not neutral, it is formation, and it forms exactly the distracted thirst Psalm 63 answers.

Early is also the resurrection's timestamp. The women who came very early at the rising of the sun were met by a stone already rolled and a tomb already empty — God had been earlier still. That is the deep comfort under the discipline: our early seeking never precedes His early helping; God shall help her, and that right early. The seeker at dawn is not initiating a meeting but arriving at one.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachar (H7836), to seek at dawn — a denominative of the word for daybreak; the LORD's own idiom of rising up early to send His prophets fills Jeremiah.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachar (H7836) — to seek early, at first light; early will I seek thee (Psa 63:1), those that seek me early shall find me (Pro 8:17).
Jeremiah's refrain — rising up early and sending — puts the same earliness in God, daily, toward a slow-hearing people (Jer 7:25).
usage: “Early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee” — dawn claimed for the deepest thirst.
“Those that seek me early shall find me” — wisdom keeps morning office hours.
“Very early in the morning… at the rising of the sun” — and the tomb was already empty.

etymology: From Latin continuus, unbroken. The Hebrew behind it, tamid, named the daily burnt offering itself — the continual.
biblical_def: Continually is the tempo of true devotion. “I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth” (Psa 34:1). The apostles structured their office around it — “we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4) — and the church its worship: “let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually” (Heb 13:15), as the first disciples “were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God” (Luk 24:53). Behind them all burns the tamid, the morning-and-evening offering that never lapsed — devotion as standing fire, not occasional spark.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines continually as without pause or cessation, unceasingly; very often, in repeated succession — the adverb of the unbroken.
webster_full: CONTINUALLY, adv. Without pause or cessation; unceasingly; as, the ocean is continually rolling its waves on the shore.
2. Very often; in repeated succession; from time to time.
scriptures: Psa 34:1
A Psalm of David, when he changed his behaviour before Abimelech; who drove him away, and he departed. I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth.
Act 6:4
But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word.
By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name.
And were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.
corruption_summary: Event-based devotion — the retreat, the conference, the streak — substituting spikes for the tamid, while the altar Scripture tends is a fire never suffered to go out.
corruption_paragraphs: The Levitical instruction under this word is precise: the fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out. Israel's worship had its feasts, but its spine was the tamid — the same lamb, morning and evening, unremarkable and unmissable. Spiritual cultures built on spikes produce saints who metabolize experiences and starve between them; the continual sacrifice of praise (Heb 13:15) is offered on ordinary Tuesdays, in the fruit of lips that keep confessing when nothing is peaking.

Acts 6:4 applies the tempo to the ministry: prayer and the word are not tasks among tasks but the continual to which the apostles gave themselves, delegating even mercy's logistics to protect it. A pastorate continually in administration and occasionally in prayer has inverted the apostolic ratio — and the congregation will eventually worship at the same tempo it is led.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamid (H8548), continuity, the daily offering — ever-burning fire, shewbread always set, the lamb morning and evening; the adverb of covenant constancy.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamid (H8548) — continually, the continual; the continual burnt offering (Exo 29:42), bread set before the LORD alway, and his praise continually in my mouth (Psa 34:1).
Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to attend constantly; they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine (Act 2:42), and we will give ourselves continually to prayer (Act 6:4).
usage: “His praise shall continually be in my mouth” — devotion as standing fire, not occasional spark.
“We will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” — the apostolic ratio.
“The sacrifice of praise to God continually” — the tamid carried into the New Covenant.

pos: v. (to come into view, be manifest; rendering Hebrew raah, Greek phaneroo)
etymology: From Latin apparere, to come forth into sight. Scripture's appearings run from the worshipper before God to the High Priest in heaven to the Lord in glory.
biblical_def: To appear is to come into view. The soul's longing: “My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?” (Psa 42:2). The present tense of our salvation: Christ entered heaven itself, “now to appear in the presence of God for us” (Heb 9:24). And the future tense: “When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory” (Col 3:4); “it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him” (1Jn 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines appear as to come or be in sight, to be in view, to become visible — and Scripture's hope is an appearing: visible glory, ours because His.
webster_full: APPEAR, v.i. To come or be in sight; to be in view; to be visible.
2. To become visible to the eye, as a spirit, or to the apprehension of the mind.
3. To stand in presence of, as parties or advocates before a court.
scriptures: Psa 42:2
My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?
Heb 9:24
For Christ is not entered into the holy places made with hands, which are the figures of the true; but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us:
Col 3:4
When Christ, who is our life, shall appear, then shall ye also appear with him in glory.
Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
corruption_summary: A culture of appearances — curated, filtered, managed — against a gospel whose three appearings (before God for us, in our hearts now, in glory at last) end the exhausting management of the self's image.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 9:24 is the believer's standing security stated as a present-tense appearing: Christ appears in the presence of God for us, now. The self-presentation industry — religious and secular — runs on the fear of how one appears before the audiences that matter; the gospel names the only Audience that finally matters and stations our Advocate in view. A conscience that knows who appears for it can stop performing for everyone else.

1 John 3:2 handles the unfinishedness modernity cannot bear: it doth not yet appear what we shall be. The believer's identity is real but not yet published; its reveal is scheduled for His appearing, and its content is likeness to Him — for we shall see him as he is. Colossians adds the hiddenness meanwhile: your life is hid with Christ in God. Hidden now, appearing then — the exact reverse of a platform age, and infinitely more restful.
roots_summary: Hebrew raah (H7200) in its passive, to be seen, to appear before God — the pilgrim verb of the feasts; Greek phaneroo (G5319), to make manifest — the verb of both advents and of our unveiling with Him.
roots_lines: Hebrew raah (H7200) — to see; niphal, to appear, be seen; three times in the year shall all thy males appear before the Lord GOD (Exo 23:17).
Greek phaneroo (G5319) — to manifest, make visible; when he shall appear (1Jn 3:2), when Christ… shall appear (Col 3:4).
Greek emphanizo (G1718) — to exhibit, present; now to appear in the presence of God for us (Heb 9:24).
usage: “When shall I come and appear before God?” — the thirst worship exists to answer.
“Now to appear in the presence of God for us” — our Advocate is in view this moment.
“When he shall appear, we shall be like him” — identity's reveal is scheduled.

pos: v. (to cover with garments; rendering Hebrew labash, Greek enduo)
etymology: From cloth, Old English clath. The Bible's first clothier is God, at the gate of Eden; its last clothing is glory.
biblical_def: To clothe is to cover. The gospel is previewed in Scripture's first clothing: “Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them” (Gen 3:21) — covering provided by God, at the cost of death, replacing fig-leaf self-covering. Isaiah sings the finished version: “he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isa 61:10). Zechariah watches it happen to a filthy high priest: “I will clothe thee with change of raiment” (Zec 3:4). And the wardrobe extends to temperament: “be clothed with humility” (1Pe 5:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clothe as to put on garments, to invest with raiment, to cover or spread over — and Scripture's deepest question is always who supplies the garment.
webster_full: CLOTHE, v.t. To put on garments; to invest the body with raiment; to cover with dress.
2. To cover or spread over; as, to clothe with verdure.
3. To furnish with raiment; to provide with clothes.
scriptures: Gen 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
Zec 3:4

And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.
Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.
corruption_summary: Fig leaves industrialized — achievement, aesthetics, and curated virtue as self-clothing — while the only covering that survives inspection is the one God cuts and puts on.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 3 stages the two rival wardrobes with permanent clarity. The first human response to guilt is manufacture: they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons. God's response is substitution: coats of skins — a death interposed — and He clothed them, the verb's subject being everything. Religion is mankind sewing; the gospel is God clothing. Zechariah 3 replays the scene judicially: Joshua stands in filthy garments, Satan at hand to accuse, and the LORD's command is not scrub harder but take away the filthy garments… I will clothe thee.

Peter's imperative — be clothed with humility — uses a rare word for the slave's apron, and the church has never outgrown the need to hear it. Even grace's wardrobe can be worn proudly; the last fitting is a garment tied on for foot-washing. The clothed-by-God are freed from self-display precisely because the robe was never theirs to weave.
roots_summary: Hebrew labash (H3847), to put on, wear, clothe — from Eden's coats to Isaiah's robe; Greek enduo (G1746), to put on — put on the Lord Jesus Christ; clothed upon with our house from heaven.
roots_lines: Hebrew labash (H3847) — to clothe, put on; the LORD God clothed them (Gen 3:21), and he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation (Isa 61:10).
Greek enduo (G1746) — to put on as a garment; put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 13:14), this mortal must put on immortality (1Co 15:53).
Greek egkomboomai (G1463) — to tie on, as a slave's apron; be clothed with humility (1Pe 5:5), its only occurrence.
usage: “Coats of skins, and clothed them” — the first covering cost a death, and God put it on.
“He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation” — righteousness worn, not woven.
“Be clothed with humility” — grace's robe finishes with a servant's apron.
